name: Ittai the Gittite
charge: As the Lord liveth, in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be
summary: David offered Ittai the Gittite, whom he called a stranger and an exile, leave to return instead of sharing his uncertain flight. Ittai swore to remain with the king in death or life and crossed with his men and their little ones. David later placed a third of the army under his command.
offense: When David fled Jerusalem, Ittai the Gittite went with him. David called him a stranger and an exile, spoke of his recent arrival, and released him from following a king who did not know where he would go (2 Samuel 15:19-20). The choice was not presented as a command to preserve Ittai's position. David gave him leave to return with his brethren. Ittai answered with an oath by the Lord and by the life of the king: wherever David should be, in death or life, there his servant would be also (2 Samuel 15:21). He accepted uncertainty when a safer course had been offered. His word did not depend upon the king first proving that he could recover Jerusalem. David told him to pass over, and Ittai crossed with his men and the little ones who were with him (2 Samuel 15:22). This was more than a favourable statement at the roadside. His company entered the journey with the displaced king while the country wept and Absalom advanced toward the city. The contrast with Absalom was sharp. David's own son sought his throne, while the man whom David had offered to release bound himself to share his danger. Nearness by household did not guarantee faithfulness, and the absence of long-standing advantage did not prevent it.
judgment: When David ordered the army for battle, he placed a third under Joab, a third under Abishai, and a third under Ittai (2 Samuel 18:2). The man who had pledged to remain with him was entrusted with a substantial command. Fidelity in flight was followed by responsibility in the defence of the kingdom. Ittai's promise had included death as well as life. It was therefore not a bargain made upon a guaranteed reward. The honour recorded afterward shows David's trust in him without changing the conditions under which he first gave his word. His place in the account preserves the value of loyalty when loyalty costs something. The throne's favour could attract many servants in Jerusalem; the road out of Jerusalem disclosed who would remain when that favour no longer promised immediate security.

verses.text: And all his servants passed on beside him; and all the Cherethites, and all the Pelethites, and all the Gittites, six hundred men which came after him from Gath, passed on before the king.
Then said the king to Ittai the Gittite, Wherefore goest thou also with us? return to thy place, and abide with the king: for thou art a stranger, and also an exile.
Whereas thou camest but yesterday, should I this day make thee go up and down with us? seeing I go whither I may, return thou, and take back thy brethren: mercy and truth be with thee.

And Ittai answered the king, and said, As the Lord liveth, and as my lord the king liveth, surely in what place my lord the king shall be, whether in death or life, even there also will thy servant be.
And David said to Ittai, Go and pass over. And Ittai the Gittite passed over, and all his men, and all the little ones that were with him.

And David sent forth a third part of the people under the hand of Joab, and a third part under the hand of Abishai the son of Zeruiah, Joab’s brother, and a third part under the hand of Ittai the Gittite. And the king said unto the people, I will surely go forth with you myself also.

entries.commentary: Absalom prepared chariots and horses and fifty men to run before him, rose up early, and stood beside the way of the gate. When any man came to the king for judgment, Absalom called him, said his matters were good and right but there was no man deputed of the king to hear him, and wished that he himself were made judge in the land that he might do every man justice. This is the sneakiness Absalom did: he began to underhand the king, winning the love of the people behind the king's back, so that he could later betray him, as the prophecy said the sword would not depart from David's house.

When any man came near to do him obeisance, Absalom put forth his hand, took him, and kissed him, and on this manner he did to all Israel that came to the king for judgment. So Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel. Instead of going to the king and resolving things, Absalom got into the king's good graces, then went around patting people on the back and stroking them. This is what the bishop calls friendish, showing people friendship without being a true friend.

After forty years Absalom asked leave to go pay his vow in Hebron, and the king said, Go in peace. But Absalom sent spies through all the tribes to say, at the sound of the trumpet, Absalom reigneth in Hebron. Two hundred men went with him from Jerusalem in their simplicity, knowing nothing. Absalom also sent for Ahithophel, David's counsellor, and the conspiracy was strong, for the people increased continually with Absalom. This shows the simplicity of a lot of brothers in Israel: a man who says all the nice things and gains favor in your eyes goes completely against leadership and out of order, and you follow along carnally, not spiritually, because he kissed your hand and told you everything would be all right.

A messenger told David the hearts of the men of Israel were with Absalom, and David told his servants to arise and flee, lest Absalom overtake them suddenly and smite the city with the sword. The king went forth with all his household, leaving ten women who were concubines to keep the house, and all his servants and the Cherethites, Pelethites, and six hundred Gittites passed on before him. David, being the man of war that he is, saw everyone starting to follow Absalom, and instead of sitting there like a dummy, chose to leave and strategize while he was out.

The king told Ittai the Gittite to return, since he was a stranger and an exile who had only just come, and wished him mercy and truth. But Ittai swore that in whatever place the king was, in death or life, there also would his servant be, so David said, Go and pass over, and Ittai passed over with all his men and little ones. All the country wept as the people passed over the brook Kidron toward the wilderness. Ittai showed a level of loyalty that David respected, so David let him come. This loyalty in the face of trouble is the same thing seen throughout Israel's story.

Zadok and all the Levites bare the ark of the covenant, and David told Zadok to carry it back into the city, saying if he found favour in the eyes of the Most High, he would be brought again to see it and its habitation; but if not, let the Most High do as seemed good. He also told Zadok the seer to return with his son Ahimaaz and Jonathan the son of Abiathar, and to send him word. So they carried the ark again to Jerusalem. David sent the ark back in faith: make sure it stays in the city, and if it is the Most High's will, I will return. That is how much faith David had. Many of the songs in the book of Psalms were written while David was on the run like this, and some of it is prophecy of Christ, because the spirit of Christ was in every prophet.

David went up the ascent of Mount Olivet weeping, barefoot, his head covered, and all the people with him weeping. When told that Ahithophel was among the conspirators, David prayed that the Most High turn Ahithophel's counsel into foolishness. Then Hushai the Archite met him with his coat rent, and David sent him back to the city to feign service to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's counsel, reporting all he heard to Zadok and Abiathar by their two sons. Ahithophel was such a good counsellor that his counsel was said to be like inquiring at the oracle of God, like talking to an angel of the Most High. So David prayed the Most High would turn that counsel into foolishness, and sent his friend Hushai to act like Absalom's servant so he could listen to Ahithophel's counsel and intervene. This was a game of chess, not checkers, and that is how we have to treat this thing today.

David numbered the people and set captains of thousands and hundreds, sending a third part under Joab, a third under Abishai, and a third under Ittai the Gittite. He said he would surely go forth with them himself. The people answered that he should not go, for he was worth ten thousand of them and it was better that he support them out of the city. David hearkened to their counsel and said what seemed best to them he would do; he did not run a dictatorship. In a time when he could not trust his own flesh and blood, he trusted the proven men he had warred with for years. David charged Joab, Abishai, and Ittai to deal gently for his sake with the young man, even with Absalom, and all the people heard the charge. Even after Absalom defiled his concubines and stole the people's hearts, David still sought to make amends with his son.

The battle was in the wood of Ephraim, and Israel was slain before the servants of David in a great slaughter of twenty thousand men. The wood devoured more people that day than the sword devoured. Absalom, riding on a mule, went under the thick boughs of a great oak, and his head caught hold of the oak so that he was taken up between the heaven and the earth while the mule went on. He hung there yet alive. A man told Joab he had seen Absalom hanged in an oak. Joab asked why he had not smitten him to the ground for a reward of ten shekels and a girdle, but the man refused, saying he would not put forth his hand against the king's son for a thousand shekels, because he had heard the king charge them to beware that none touch the young man. The man told Joab that to have killed Absalom would have been to work falsehood against his own life, for nothing is hid from the king, and Joab himself would have set himself against him. Joab said he would not tarry, took three darts, and thrust them through the heart of Absalom while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak. Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bore Joab's armor compassed Absalom and smote him and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

Joab blew the trumpet and held back the people from pursuing Israel. They took Absalom, cast him into a great pit in the woods, and laid a very great heap of stones upon him, and all Israel fled everyone to his tent. In his lifetime Absalom had reared up a pillar for himself in the king's dale, saying he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and he called it after his own name; it is called Absalom's place unto this day.

Ahimaaz wanted to run and bear the king the tidings that the Lord had avenged him of his enemies, but Joab first sent Cushi, since the king's son was dead and this was not good news to carry. Ahimaaz pressed again and was allowed to run, and he outran Cushi by way of the plain. David sat between the two gates while the watchman on the wall saw first Ahimaaz running alone, then another man. The king said a man running alone brings tidings, and he recognized the running of Ahimaaz as a good man coming with good news. Ahimaaz fell before the king and said all was well, blessing the Lord who had delivered up the men that lifted their hand against the king; the good news was that David was alive and had overcome. When David asked if the young man Absalom was safe, Ahimaaz said he saw a great tumult but knew not what it was. Cushi came and said the enemies of the king and all that rose against him should be as that young man is. David understood that his son was one of the casualties of war. He was much moved, went up to the chamber over the gate, and wept, crying, O my son Absalom, would God I had died for thee. David's whole life was war, slaughtering giants from his youth up, and now he mourned in heartache for his son.
